questions.q: A JWT is three Base64url parts joined by dots. What is the correct order?
o: payload.header.signature
header.payload.signature
signature.header.payload
header.signature.payload
questions.x: The format is always header.payload.signature. Each part is Base64url encoded. The signature is computed over the first two parts, so it comes last.
questions.h: The signature is calculated from the other two parts. That computed value has to sit at the end.

questions.q: Is Base64url encoding the same as encryption for a JWT payload?
o: Yes, reversing it requires the same key that signed the token
No, anyone can decode the payload without a key or extra secret
Only JWT-specific libraries can reverse Base64url on payloads
Yes, but only the payload segment is encrypted by Base64url
questions.x: Base64url is an encoding scheme, not encryption. It makes the JSON safe to put in cookies and URLs, but the original claims are fully readable after a decode.
questions.h: Ask whether a secret key is required to reverse base64. Try decoding any JWT payload in a terminal.

questions.q: What critical step does this lab's server skip before trusting JWT claims?
o: Checking the exp timestamp against the current time
Verifying the cryptographic signature on the token
Decoding the Base64url payload into JSON claims
Checking the iss claim against a configured issuer
questions.x: The server reads the payload and acts on it, but never checks whether the signature is valid. A forged payload therefore passes through unchallenged.
questions.h: The server does decode and use the payload. What cryptographic check does it forget before trusting those claims?

questions.q: Which JWT payload claim identifies the logged-in user in this lab?
o: iss
iat
sub
exp
questions.x: The sub (subject) claim carries the username. Changing it from wiener to administrator impersonates the admin, because the server never validates the signature.
questions.h: You need to change the username. Look for the claim whose name is short for subject.

questions.q: After the payload is edited, what is true of the original JWT signature?
o: The library recalculates it automatically on every decode
It no longer matches, but this server accepts it anyway
The server rejects the token because the signature is now invalid
The signature is stripped out automatically during re-encoding
questions.x: The signature no longer matches the modified payload, so it is cryptographically invalid. This server never checks it, so the mismatch does not matter.
questions.h: The signature was computed over the original bytes. Does this server ever look at that signature?

questions.q: What is the minimum work needed to forge a JWT when signature checks are skipped?
o: Crack the signing key, then re-sign the modified token
Decode the payload, change a claim, re-encode, and reassemble
Delete the signature so the token has only two dotted parts
Set alg to none in the header and drop every payload claim
questions.x: No key is required. Decode the payload, change sub, Base64url-encode it again, and reassemble header, new payload, and the original signature. The server accepts it.
questions.h: No cracking is required. The server never checks signatures, so you only need to deal with the encoding layer.

questions.q: How does this lab send the JWT to the server on authenticated requests?
o: A custom X-Auth-Token header on every request
The session cookie, whose value is the JWT string
A query parameter named token on every page URL
A JSON sessionToken field in the request body
questions.x: After login, the Set-Cookie header stores the JWT as the session cookie. Forged tokens are sent the same way with a Cookie header on later requests.
questions.h: Look at the login response headers. Where does the browser store the token it then repeats on every request?

questions.q: Which of the following is true of forging the admin token in this lab?
o: The captured JWT uses RS256 even though the signature is never checked
All of these statements are true about this unverified signature lab
Only the middle payload segment needs to be replaced after editing
The original header and signature can stay in the forged token
questions.x: The token is RS256, but verification is skipped, so the algorithm never matters. Only sub in the payload changes. Header and signature stay as captured.
questions.h: Recall what the decoded header showed, which JWT part you actually edited, and whether you re-signed.

questions.q: Which tool is commonly used to inspect JWT header and payload in a browser?
o: Wireshark, for reading JWT bytes from captured TCP streams
jwt.io, a debugger that decodes headers and payloads visually
Postman, for storing JWT strings only as environment variables
Burp Decoder, which treats JWTs as raw Base64 with no claims view
questions.x: jwt.io decodes the header and payload in a browser and can re-encode edits. It is handy for inspection even when you later forge tokens in a script.
questions.h: The tool lives at a domain named after the token format itself. It is the usual first search result for JWT decoder.

questions.q: What is the correct server-side fix for this unverified-signature failure?
o: Encrypt the payload so attackers cannot read the JSON claims
Verify the signature against the expected key before trusting claims
Use HTTPS so the token cannot be stolen on the network path
Add an exp claim without ever checking the cryptographic signature
questions.x: The root fix is mandatory signature verification. If the library path skips verify, the token gives no authentication guarantee, regardless of HTTPS or exp.
questions.h: The attack works because verification is skipped. What is the logical fix for code that skips that check?
